source.title: Deep Causal Transcoding: A Framework for Mechanistically Eliciting Latent Behaviors in Language Models

record.tranche_reason: The post uses ideas from computation in superposition to motivate its calibration procedure, but its experiments study DCT steering and jailbreak elicitation rather than testing the stated superposition claims.
record.gate_note: The post reports DCT feature geometry and effects of adding or ablating learned directions; these are recorded under fits_no_version because they do not test the specific versions listed. Excluded the DCT activation-function comparisons and password-locked capability results because they do not measure the claim's representation or geometry. The jailbreak scores are effects of deliberately applied steering or ablation, not evidence that these behaviors occur without intervention.
record.test_reason: The post builds a steering-vector method (deep causal transcoders) motivated partly by computation-in-superposition and non-orthogonal feature arguments. Its results are jailbreak scores and the geometry of its own learned steering directions. It reports no toy-model superposition, no neuron polysemanticity, no SAE features and no test of feature dimensionality. The better generalization of non-orthogonal DCTs is the method's own performance, not a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The author concludes exponential DCTs give the most generalizable steering vectors, attributing this to non-orthogonal features. The author gives suggestive, non-conclusive evidence for >200 harmless directions, plus a hypothesized single primary refusal direction. The record's added sentence about canonical features is the reader's framing, not the author's conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The post develops deep causal transcoders and evaluates steering and ablation in language models; it does not reproduce the toy-network setup or measurements of Toy Models of Superposition.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported jailbreak outcomes differ between activation addition and directional ablation, and between individual and aggregated directions.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen1.5-7B-Chat, 240 DCT input directions elicit jailbreaks. Their condition number is ~38 and mean absolute pairwise dot product is .36 (SD .19). Output directions have mean dot product .25 and condition number 27 (author comment).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: One behavioral concept (harmlessness) can be causally triggered by many non-collinear, loosely correlated directions (feature multiplicity).

fits_no_version.finding: Averaged directions beat the mean but not the best individual direction when added (9.80/10.31 vs 14.19). When ablated, averaged directions beat the best individual one (7.30/6.78 vs 5.94; target layer 2.55/2.90 vs 1.73).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal may be mediated by one primary in-distribution direction plus many secondary directions that elicit jailbreaks under addition.

record.problems: The author describes the evidence for feature multiplicity as suggestive and not conclusive. The 240-vector analysis is based on one stated run; the post does not report repeated-run uncertainty for these geometry measurements. The jailbreak score is a proxy, and the author notes that its relation to actual jailbreak behavior may be imperfect.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-bearing result rows were left out. Other sections report DCT jailbreak or capability-elicitation results, but those measure induced behaviors rather than the representation claims cataloged here.

untested.parts: Toy networks, sparsity-dependent transition, feature geometry in toy settings: all untested.
Capacity competition as the cause of polysemanticity: untested.
Non-capacity origins of polysemantic neurons: untested.
No neuron-level distribution or SAE recovery of sparse features is measured. DCT directions are causal steering directions, not sparse features.
No SAE features are evaluated. The post only argues SAEs may miss out-of-distribution features, without results.
The DCT assumes 1-D gating directions; the dimensionality of features is not tested.

missing.what: Output-direction (u) geometry for the same 240 factors: mean absolute dot product .25, condition number 27. This bears on the feature-multiplicity finding, not on any version.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'assumes' to 'uses_without_test'. The post uses superposition theory to justify non-orthogonal feature learning and the calibration of R, but tests no version. The comparison of linear vs quadratic vs exponential DCTs is the method's own benchmark and was rightly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular feature geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The post measures learned steering directions, not features spread across neurons or sparse features recovered by an SAE.
No SAE features are evaluated for completeness, stability, or canonical status.

The DCT represents learned effects using one-dimensional directions, but the study does not test whether the model's underlying features are intrinsically one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.
